prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Trailing her father, bearing his hand axe, the girl thought she had never guessed what earthly majesty was before then, as he strode unconcernedly holding a vicious gander by the horny mitts and let the big wings batter his knees. She was also surprised to feel a liberating satisfaction in the coming bloodshed, and that notwithstanding all the times she had been beleaguered and had fled, today she did not fear the barnyard hubub. Yet, as her father’s clever stroke fell, as the pronged head skipped sideways and the neck plumes stiffened with blood from the cleft, she was angry; and, when the headless goose ran to the brook and was carried off into the woods alive, she rejoiced, and subsequently frequented those woods and avoided her father. When the goose began to mend she brought him small hominy, which was welcome though she had to press the kernels one by one into the pink neck that throbbed into her palm; when haemorrhage occurred she would not spare handkerchiefs, and stanching the spot she felt a thrill of sympathy. But for the most part there was steady progress, and growing vigor was accompanied by restlessness, and one cool day the blind thing was batted out of existence by a motorcycle. She had no time for tears. She ran upstairs to miss her father’s barytone commiseration, then out onto the fields, and, holding an old red pinwheel, ran ran ran ran.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A young girl, initially awed by her father's brutal efficiency in beheading a gander for slaughter, feels an unexpected surge of anger and secretly nurses the surviving, headless bird back in the woods, feeding it grain and staunching its bleeding by hand. When a motorcycle finally kills the creature, she flees not into grief but into frantic, wordless motion across the fields—revealing how her tenderness toward suffering ultimately exceeds her capacity to mourn or articulate loss.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Trailing, She, Yet

outputs.L1:
Trailing her father, bearing his hand axe, the girl thought she had never before glimpsed such earthly majesty as he displayed, striding unconcernedly with a vicious gander gripped by its horny feet, the great wings battering against his knees. She was startled, too, to feel a liberating satisfaction rising within her at the coming bloodshed—and that despite all the times she had been beleaguered and had fled, she felt no fear today of the barnyard's clamor. Yet when her father's clever stroke fell, when the pronged head skipped sideways and the neck plumes stiffened with blood welling from the cleft, she was seized with anger; and when the headless goose ran to the brook and was carried off, still alive, into the woods, she rejoiced—and thereafter she haunted those woods and kept her distance from her father.

When the goose began to mend, she brought him small portions of hominy, which he welcomed, though she had to press the kernels one by one into the pink, throbbing neck that pulsed against her palm. When hemorrhage occurred, she spared no handkerchiefs, and in stanching the wound she felt a thrill of tenderness. For the most part, though, his recovery was steady, and his growing vigor brought with it a restlessness—until one cool day the blind creature was struck out of existence by a passing motorcycle.

She had no time for tears. She fled upstairs to escape her father's baritone condolences, then out into the fields, where, clutching an old red pinwheel, she ran and ran and ran and ran.
outputs.L2:
Walking behind her father, carrying his small axe, the girl realized she had never before witnessed such earthly grandeur as he displayed, striding calmly while gripping a fierce gander by its rough, scaly feet, allowing the powerful wings to strike against his legs. Unexpectedly, she found herself experiencing a freeing sense of satisfaction at the violence about to unfold, and despite countless previous occasions when she'd been overwhelmed by fear and had run from the chaos of the barnyard, this particular day held no dread for her.

However, the moment her father's skilled blow landed—when the forked head bounced to one side and the throat feathers turned rigid with blood pouring from the wound—fury rose within her. Then, watching the decapitated bird dash toward the stream and vanish still living into the forest beyond, joy overtook her instead. From that point forward, she began wandering those same woods repeatedly, keeping her distance from her father.

Once the goose started healing, she would bring him tiny bits of hominy corn—food he accepted gladly, though she had to feed him kernel by kernel directly into his pulsing pink throat. During episodes of bleeding, she never hesitated to sacrifice her handkerchiefs, and as she pressed against the wound to stop the flow, a wave of tenderness moved through her.

For the most part, however, the bird's condition steadily improved, his growing strength bringing with it an increasing restlessness. Then, on a chilly afternoon, a passing motorcycle struck and killed the sightless creature instantly.

She didn't pause to weep. Instead, she dashed upstairs, avoiding her father's deep-voiced expressions of sympathy, before rushing back outside into the open fields where, clutching a weathered red pinwheel, she ran and ran and ran and ran.
outputs.L3:
The girl stood at the edge of the yard, watching her father's hands close around the gander's neck with a casualness that seemed to belong to some older, harder world. There was no hesitation in him, no flicker of doubt—only the practiced economy of a man who had done this a hundred times before and would do it a hundred times again. She watched the muscles in his forearms tighten, watched the bird's wings beat once, twice, against the air in a final, futile protest, and felt something close to reverence rise in her chest. This was power. This was violence made ordinary, folded into the fabric of an afternoon like laundry or firewood, and she could not look away.

Ordinarily the barnyard frightened her—the shrieking of geese defending their territory, the sudden rush of wings, the way the whole flock could turn hostile in an instant. She had learned to keep her distance, to flatten herself against the fence when the ganders hissed. But today was different. Today there was no fear in her, only a strange, unfamiliar lightness, as though the violence about to unfold might loosen something that had been coiled too tight inside her for too long. She wanted to see the blood. She wanted release, though she could not have named it as such, and the wanting itself felt like a kind of freedom.

But the killing did not go as her father intended. The axe fell, the head separated from the body—and still the goose ran. It fled headless into the tree line, wings pumping, legs carrying it in a last delirious sprint away from the stump and the blade and the man who stood there, momentarily as stunned as his daughter. She felt her stomach twist with anger at what he had done, at the violence she had so recently admired now made grotesque and unbearable. And yet beneath the anger, something else bloomed: joy, fierce and unreasoning, that the goose had escaped. That it had refused to die on command.

She found it two days later, alive against all sense, blundering blind through the underbrush at the edge of the property. From that day she became its secret keeper. She brought it grain in her cupped hands, water in an old tin cup, and she learned to move quietly past her father's line of sight, to slip out to the tree line when his back was turned or his attention elsewhere. She could not have explained why she needed to save this particular bird, why its survival mattered more than anything else that summer, only that it did, and that the secrecy of the tending made it feel like something sacred, something entirely her own.

Weeks passed, and the bond between them deepened in the strange, wordless way that bonds form between the wounded and their keepers. The goose could not see her coming, could only sense her by sound and smell, by the rhythm of her footsteps and the particular gentleness of her hands as she cleaned the ragged wound where its head had been. It grew restless as it healed, straining against the rope she'd tied loosely to keep it near, flapping and stumbling in circles, and still she loved it—loved its blindness, its stubbornness, its refusal to simply lie down and be finished.

Then, one afternoon, a motorcycle came tearing down the lane past the property, and the goose, disoriented and unhearing in the way it had always been since that first blow, wandered into its path. It was over in a moment—a sound, a silence, and then nothing.

Her father came toward her afterward, arms open, his face arranged into something like sorrow, something like apology. But she could not go to him. Could not let him fold her into the same hands that had first raised the axe. Instead she turned and ran, out past the barn and the fence line and into the open fields where the grass moved in long silver waves under the wind. She ran until her lungs burned, until the farmhouse was small behind her, and there, alone, she stopped and stood clutching a pinwheel she had picked up without thinking—its plastic vanes ticking uselessly in the breeze—while the grief broke open inside her, raw and wordless, too large yet for any shape but silence.
outputs.L4:
# The Gander

The axe came down clean. That was the first thing Marta understood about her father—that he did nothing halfway, that his hands, which she had watched shell peas and mend fences and once, memorably, catch a falling swallow's nest before it shattered on the stone step, could also bring an axe down on the stretched neck of a gander with the same unhurried precision he used for everything else. She had been sent to fetch water and had stopped instead at the corner of the barn, water forgotten, watching the bird's white body convulse in the dust while her father wiped the blade on his trouser leg and called for the next one.

She was eight. She did not yet have words for what moved in her chest—something between admiration and horror, the two so tangled she could not have separated them if asked. Her father was strong. Her father was necessary. The farm needed geese killed in autumn the way it needed rain in spring, and no one else questioned this, least of all the geese, who went to the block with the same placid stupidity they brought to everything.

Except one did not go quite the way it should have.

The axe missed its full mark—perhaps her father was tired, perhaps the bird twisted at the wrong moment—and instead of the clean separation he intended, something else happened: the gander, though grievously wounded, rose up from the block in a spray of blood and ran. It ran the way headless things are said to run in old stories, blind and undirected, wings beating uselessly, and it did not stop until it had crossed half the yard and collapsed against the fence.

Her father swore, wiped his hands, and went to finish the job—but Marta was already moving, faster than she had moved for anything in her life, and she reached the bird first.

"Leave it," her father said. "It's dead already. It just doesn't know it."

But it was not dead. She could feel that beneath her hands, the frantic heat of its body, the pulse still driving blood through what remained of it. She did not think about what she was doing. She only knew that she could not let her father's axe finish what his hands had begun to unmake, and so she gathered the bird—heavy, wet, terrible—against her apron and ran with it into the trees at the field's edge, where the light went green and dim and no one would think to look for a girl who had only gone, as far as anyone knew, to fetch water she had never fetched.

---

What she did in the woods over the following days she could not have explained to anyone, least of all herself. She was not a sentimental child; she had watched animals die before, had eaten what her father killed without particular grief, understood in some unarticulated way that this was simply how a farm continued. But something in the sight of that headless, running bird had cracked open a place in her that she had not known existed, and now she could not close it again.

She fed the gander grain, softened with water, pressing it into the ragged opening where its head had been, though she barely knew if this served any purpose beyond her own need to do something. She packed the wound with moss when it bled, held her small hands against the raw place until the blood slowed and something like a scab began to form. The bird could not eat in any way she understood eating, could not see, could not, presumably, know in any sense that a girl knelt beside it every day pressing grain-paste into its ruined neck—and yet it lived. It lived for one day, and then another, moving in slow blind circles at the end of a cord she had tied loosely around its leg and fastened to a stake, walking the small orbit of its captivity with the same aimless persistence it might have shown foraging in the yard.

She told no one. This was not difficult; her father, having written the bird off as a loss, did not think to count his flock and notice the discrepancy, and her mother, occupied with younger children and the endless business of the house, did not ask why Marta was so often missing in the afternoons, her apron stained in ways she did not explain.

She did not think of what she was doing as love, though it may have been the nearest thing to it she had yet practiced. She only knew that she could not let the bird simply stop, that its persistence in living, however diminished, however senseless, demanded some answering persistence from her. Each day she expected to find it dead, curled in the leaf-litter with the flies already finding it, and each day it was instead standing, swaying faintly, waiting in whatever manner a headless thing could be said to wait, for the grain and water and the pressure of her hands.

---

It was a boy on a motorcycle who ended it—not maliciously, not even carelessly in any way he could be blamed for, since the machine came down the lane behind the trees at a speed no one could have anticipated, and the gander, startled perhaps by the sound, or simply moving in its blind circuit at the wrong moment, wandered into the path of the wheel.

Marta heard it before she saw it: the engine's snarl, then a sound she would spend years trying not to remember, and by the time she reached the lane the boy had already gone, unaware, roaring off toward town without the smallest knowledge of what he had left behind him in the dust.

The bird was very still. It had never, in all the days she tended it, achieved a stillness like this, and something in her recognized instantly that this was different, that this was the stillness she had been holding off with grain and moss and the pressure of her palms, arrived now despite everything she had done.

She did not kneel beside it. She did not touch it, or gather it up as she had gathered it that first day, or do any of the things a child in a story might do when confronted with the death of something she had labored to save. Instead she turned and ran—not toward the house, not toward her mother or father or anyone who might offer the shape of comfort, but out across the open field, running in no particular direction, her arms pumping, her breath tearing at her chest, running as though speed itself might outdistance what had happened, might convert grief into mere motion before it could settle into her and become something she would have to carry.

She ran until the field gave way to another field, and then another, until her legs ached and her lungs burned and the light began to slant toward evening, and even then she did not stop to weep, did not sink down into the grass and give the moment its due of tears. She simply ran, and ran, as if outrunning were itself a kind of tending, as if the same hands that had staunched blood and pressed grain into a wound might now, having nothing left to save, find no other use for themselves than this: the body given over entirely to motion, because stillness—now, finally—was the one thing she could not bear.
outputs.L5:
# Trailing Light

She walked along the shoreline as the sun began its slow descent, her shadow trailing behind her like a companion made of dusk. The waves lapped rhythmically against the sand, erasing footprints as quickly as they formed—yet something about this ritual felt permanent, as if the ocean remembered every step even as it smoothed them away.

She had come here searching for clarity, trailing threads of thought that refused to weave into anything coherent. Questions about her future hung in the air like gulls circling overhead, restless and unanswered. Yet there was comfort in the uncertainty, in not knowing exactly where the path would lead.

The evening light cast long shadows across the beach, trailing gold across the water in shimmering ribbons. She paused, watching the horizon swallow the sun whole. Yet even as darkness crept in, she felt no fear—only a quiet anticipation for whatever trailed behind this moment, waiting patiently in the wings of tomorrow.

She turned finally toward home, her footsteps trailing a path back through the dunes. Yet she carried something different with her now than what she'd brought—a sense of peace that had been trailing her all along, waiting only to be noticed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, densely lyrical prose piece in the style of Southern Gothic fiction about a young girl watching her father behead a goose, only for the bird to survive headless for a while before dying suddenly.
counterfactuals.output:
The morning came up the color of a healed wound, pink and thin, and the girl sat on the porch step with her knees drawn to her chest and watched her daddy carry the goose out by its feet like a lantern he meant to hang somewhere far from the house.

The block was gray oak, silvered with old blood gone the color of rust in rain. He did not speak. He never spoke for this. He held the goose down with the flat of his forearm, and the bird's eye rolled once toward the girl, black and wet as a well you could fall into and never hit bottom, and then the hatchet came down with a sound like a door closing in another room.

The head fell into the grass and lay there being nothing, being just a small strange stone with a beak.

But the body did not know yet. That was the thing nobody told you, the thing her mother's Bible didn't mention between all its begettings and its endings—that death took its time arriving, that it came up through the legs slow as a rumor moving through a town. The goose stood. It took one step, then another, wings unlatching from its sides like something trying to remember what flight was for. It ran a small crooked circuit around the yard, white feathers catching the early sun, blood roping out behind it in a long red ribbon that wrote itself into the dirt and then erased itself, wrote itself and erased itself, some sentence with no verb, no end.

The girl did not look away. Something in her had gone still and old, the way a held breath gets old, waiting.

Her daddy stood with the hatchet loose in his hand, watching too, his face unreadable as scripture in a language no one living spoke anymore.

The goose ran until it did not. It happened without warning, the way weather changes—one moment the wings beating their frantic hymn against the air, and the next, the body simply stopping, folding down into the grass like a sheet someone had finished with, like it had only just then received the news and could not bear to carry it standing up.

The silence afterward had a weight to it. The kind that presses on the chest.

The girl looked at the head lying separate in the grass, and at the body lying separate near the fence, and understood for the first time that a thing could go on for a while after it was already over—that the leaving and the being-gone were not the same moment, not the same country, and that a soul might linger in its ruined house long after the roof had fallen, walking its familiar rooms out of habit, before it finally believed enough to lie down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you craft a literary vignette with archaic, Faulkner-esque syntax where a child feels conflicting awe, anger, and tenderness after witnessing an animal beheading on a farm?
counterfactuals.output:
The hatchet fell and did not so much sever as *conclude*, the way a sentence concludes, the way his grandfather's voice concluded of a Sunday when the reading was done and the book closed with that same terrible finality, and the boy standing there in the chicken-yard dust that was not dust now but was going red, going redder, thought: *this is what an ending looks like*, and did not move, could not move, his bare feet rooted there as if the earth itself had reached up through them and claimed some kinship with what lay twitching, headless, its wings beating against nothing, against the very air that had once held it up and now seemed to hold it down, pressing, pressing, until the beating stopped and there was only the wings lying open like a book someone had abandoned mid-sentence.

He hated then—hated the grandfather with his rolled sleeves and his hands that did not shake, hated the sun for continuing its indifferent arc, hated the red wheelbarrow waiting there for the body as if it had known all along, as if the whole yard, the whole farm, the whole telluric weight of the world had conspired toward this single moment of blade and bone—and yet.

And yet.

He loved him too, the old man, loved the way his grandfather knelt after, not in prayer exactly but in something adjacent to it, loved the rough certainty of those hands as they plucked the first feathers, loved even the blood drying black on the packed earth because it was *necessary*, because the necessary was its own kind of grace, was it not, was it not the same grace that let the boy eat come Sunday, the same grace that had fed him every day of his short life without his ever once considering the small savage ceremonies required to sustain it—

and he wept then, not from grief exactly, not only, but from the terrible understanding that had come upon him all at once like weather, like a storm crossing a field before you have time to run for the house: that tenderness and violence were not opposites but were rather two hands on the same haft, two words for the same old necessary thing, and that he would spend the whole of his life, the whole remainder of his days, trying to hold both without letting either one go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a story inspired by the real-life "headless chicken" phenomenon, told through the eyes of a farmer's daughter who nurses the surviving bird until it dies in an ironic, modern accident.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Rooster Knew

My father cut the heads off sixteen chickens that morning, and I know this because I counted the buckets. Sixteen buckets, sixteen thuds against the chopping stump, sixteen headless bodies that ran in their brief, meaningless circles before folding into the grass. I was nine years old and had seen it before, had learned not to flinch, had learned that this was simply what Saturdays were for.

The seventeenth was different.

My father told it later like a joke he didn't understand the punchline to: the axe fell a little high, missed the jugular, spared just enough of the brain stem that something in the bird refused to accept its own arithmetic. It didn't run in circles. It stood. It shook itself the way chickens do after rain, as though shrugging off something that didn't belong to it, and then it walked — actually walked, with intention — toward the water trough and tried to drink through a throat that no longer existed above the collarbone.

My father, a practical man who did not believe in signs, nearly finished the job with a hatchet on the spot. I was the one who grabbed his sleeve.

I don't know why. I have turned that moment over so many times in the years since, trying to find the version of myself who made that choice, and I still don't fully trust my own memory of it. What I remember is that the bird was still *standing*, still tilting what remained of its neck toward the sun like it was listening for something, and it seemed unbearably wrong to end a thing that was so clearly trying not to end.

We called him Chance. Not for luck, exactly — more like an acknowledgment that something had simply rolled the wrong way, and here we all were, having to live with it.

---

The feeding was the hard part. My father rigged an eyedropper from the barn's veterinary kit, and twice a day I'd tilt Chance backward — he never fought me, which still unsettles me to think about — and drip a mixture of water, milk, and softened grain down the open pipe of his esophagus, careful to avoid what my father called "the wrong hole," meaning the one that led to his lungs. I got good at it. I could do it one-handed by the second week, humming to him the way you'd hum to an infant, though I couldn't have told you what a headless rooster might find soothing.

He kept his balance by learning to lean. He'd press the stump of his neck against the corner post of his pen, and I swear — I *swear* — there was a kind of peace in the posture. Chickens are not thoughtful animals. I'd spent my whole childhood among them and never once suspected they had inner lives worth speaking of. But Chance developed habits, preferences, what I can only call moods. He hated Tuesdays, when the tractor ran past his pen. He liked to be near the other hens, though they mostly ignored him, pecking at feed he'd never taste again.

Word got out the way it does in small towns — through the feed store, through church, through my mother's sister who worked at the paper. A reporter came, then a television crew from three counties over, then a man from a website who wanted to film Chance for what he called "content," a phrase that made my father's jaw tighten in a way I didn't understand until years later. Strangers sent checks. Strangers sent hate mail, accusing us of torturing an animal that should have been allowed to die with dignity. Strangers sent prayers, as though Chance were a saint and not a rooster with an unfortunate anatomy and an uncooperative axe.

I didn't care about any of it. I cared about the dropper, the grain, the leaning post, the particular way Chance's remaining wing would twitch when I came into the coop each morning — a gesture I chose to interpret as recognition, though I'll never know if that was true or only what a lonely girl needed to believe.

He lived four hundred and eleven days. I know because I marked them on the inside of the feed shed door in pencil, a tally that grew embarrassingly long, that my father eventually painted over without asking me, as though erasing the number might make the whole business feel less strange to the neighbors who still slowed their trucks as they passed our fence line.

---

He did not die from any complication of his condition. That's the part people always want to hear about, and the part that still catches in my throat like a bone.

My father, in the manner of men who cannot leave well enough alone, had gotten it into his head that our operation needed modernizing. A cousin sold him on an automatic coop system — timed doors, motion-sensor feeders, the whole apparatus wired to a small control box that my father was inordinately proud of, though he never fully learned to program it and left the factory settings running most of the time.

I was seventeen by then. Chance had long since become simply a fact of our farm, the way the crooked fence post was a fact, the way my mother's cough each November was a fact. I still fed him by hand out of habit and love, though the automatic feeder made it technically unnecessary. I think I understood, even then, that the feeding was for me as much as for him.

The coop door was meant to lower at seven each evening, sealing the hens in against foxes and weather. It had done this without incident for three months. On an ordinary Thursday in October, with no wind, no malfunction anyone could later explain to my satisfaction, the door's timer fired four minutes early — while Chance stood in the frame, leaning as he always leaned, waiting perhaps for nothing at all, the way he waited for everything.

There is no elegant way to say what a steel door falling at that speed does to a body already missing so much of itself. I found him at dusk. My father found me sitting beside him in the dirt, not crying yet, just sitting, running the arithmetic of it in a way that felt almost funny, in the way that terrible things sometimes do before the grief catches up: that a bird who had shrugged off the axe, who had out-stubborned death itself for over a year, who had survived becoming a curiosity and a headline and a small local miracle — had been undone at last not by nature, not by God, not even by my father's original mistake, but by a machine my father had bought to make our lives easier.

I have told this story at dinner parties, in the careless tone people use for things they've decided to find funny. I laugh in the right places. I say *you can't make this up* and *the irony practically writes itself*, and people laugh too, and we move on to other subjects.

But some nights I still think of him leaning into that post, patient in a way no living thing should have needed to be, waiting on a world that had already taken the very thing that should have let him rest — and I think that if there is a lesson in it, it isn't about fate, or miracles, or the strange durability of animal bodies.

It's that the things we build to spare us from tragedy have a way of becoming, eventually, its instrument. That survival is not the same as safety. That I fed a headless bird by hand for four hundred and eleven days, and loved him, in whatever strange shape love takes when it's poured drop by drop down an open throat — and none of that tenderness was any match, in the end, for a door that didn't know what it was closing on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a piece of flash fiction with a dark, almost mythic tone: a girl admires her father's brutal skill in a barnyard task, then secretly cares for the maimed animal, ending with her fleeing across a field.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Keeping

Her father moved through the herd like something out of an older story, one hand cupped beneath the ram's jaw, the other dark with the small knife he kept for this. The animal did not fight him. None of them ever did, in the end—as if some old bargain passed between man and beast the moment his palm found their throat, promising quickness in exchange for stillness.

The ram had broken fence three times that month, led the ewes into the corn, cost them half a field. So her father did what was done in such cases, what his father had done before him and his father's father: he laid the animal down in the trampled grass and cut the tendon behind its hock, clean as opening a letter. The ram screamed once, a sound she would carry for years, then went silent, breathing hard, its back leg already useless, already forgiven.

She watched from the fence rail, nine years old, and felt something bloom in her chest that she did not have a word for yet—not joy, not exactly, but a fierce, private awe at how little her father's hands trembled, how the whole brutal act took less time than saying grace. He straightened, wiped the blade on his thigh, glanced at her without expression, and walked back toward the house as though he'd only mended a boot.

That night she went out with a lantern she wasn't supposed to touch and found the ram where they'd left it, in the far corner of the barn, dragging itself in circles at the end of its tether. It flinched from her light, then didn't. She knelt and pressed her palm to the wound, the way she'd seen her mother do with a burned hand, and the ram let her, shivering, its eye rolling white and enormous in the dark.

She came back every night after that. She brought water in a chipped bowl, brought bread softened with milk, packed the wound with the yarrow that grew wild by the creek because she'd heard once, from a woman at church, that it stopped the rot. She never told her father. She didn't know, then, what she was hiding, or from whom—only that the tending had become its own ritual, as private and necessary as his cutting had been public.

The ram lived. It healed crooked, dragging its bad leg through the mud, marked forever as a thing that had been punished and kept. Her father regarded it sometimes across the pen with something like satisfaction—see, it hadn't needed killing, only correcting—and she understood, with a cold drop in her stomach, that this was the whole of his mercy: not to spare, but to maim precisely enough that the maiming became a kind of use.

She was eleven the night she woke to voices below—her father's, flat and final, and the low complaint of the ram being led out past the smokehouse toward the winter cull. She did not remember deciding to run. She only remembered the door swinging wide beneath her hand, the cold shocking her bare feet, and then the field opening before her, black and enormous under a moon like a knife-blade left out to dry.

She ran without looking back, the wet grass whipping her ankles, the dark barn shrinking behind her into something small enough to survive, and somewhere far off a lantern moved, and somewhere closer her own breath tore ragged from her throat—not away from her father, not exactly, but from the terrible, familiar tenderness she had learned at his hand: that to keep a thing alive and to ruin it were sometimes the very same mercy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a highly stylized short narrative (think Flannery O'Connor) about innocence, violence, and grief on a farm, culminating in the girl running through the fields holding a pinwheel after the animal's sudden death.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Pinwheel

The goat died on a Tuesday, which Lacey Ann would remember later as the kind of ordinary day that had no business holding something so large. Her daddy found it in the lower pasture, its throat opened up like a purse spilling something dark and final into the clover, and he stood there a long time with his hat in his hands like a man at church who'd forgotten the words to the hymn everybody else was singing.

"Dogs," he said, though there were no dogs on the Pruitt place, hadn't been since the flood took the hound in '61. But a man needs a word for the thing that comes in the night and takes what's his, and dogs was as good a word as any.

Lacey Ann was nine and had named the goat Sister, on account of it followed her everywhere the way a sister might, if she'd had one, which she didn't, her mother having stopped after her like the Lord had drawn a line under Lacey Ann's name and closed the book.

She did not cry when she saw Sister in the grass. She had a pinwheel in her hand, orange and yellow, that her granddaddy had brought back from the feed store, and she held it very still so the blades wouldn't turn, as if stillness might travel backward through the morning and stop whatever had happened from happening.

Her mother came out onto the porch with flour on her hands and asked was everything all right, and her daddy said go on back inside, and something in the way he said it made the whole farm go quiet — even the chickens, even the wind, which had been busy all morning turning things.

That was when Lacey Ann ran.

She did not run away from the goat so much as into the rest of the world, the pinwheel held out before her like a torch or a flag or a small sun she was personally responsible for keeping lit. The blades caught the air and screamed their thin plastic scream, orange and yellow, orange and yellow, and she ran through the low pasture where the grass was wet with what she would not let herself call blood, and through the fence line where the wire had rusted to the color of dried apricots, and out into the field where the corn stood taller than her father and rattled like something trying to tell her a secret it didn't have the words for either.

She ran until her lungs turned to two small fists inside her chest, until the pinwheel was just a blur of color she trusted more than she trusted her own eyes, until she could not hear her mother calling or her father's shovel starting its slow work against the earth.

She ran because Sister could not, not anymore, and someone on that farm needed to be moving, needed to be proof that the legs still worked, that the wind still turned things bright and ordinary, that a girl could hold a small machine of joy in her fist and let it spin and spin and spin against a sky that did not care one way or another what was buried by sundown.

Behind her, the farm did what farms do. It kept its silence. It let the corn have the last word.
